params.why: the fraction is in lowest terms, so its decimal has exactly one digit before a recurring pair

stem: Write ${=w}\frac{{=n}}{{=d}}$ in decimal form, using dot notation for the recurring digits.
solution: The whole number ${=w}$ stays as it is, so we only need $\frac{{=n}}{{=d}}$ as a decimal. Divide ${=n}$ by ${=d}$ by long division, bringing down a zero each time, until a remainder comes back.
$10 \times {=n} = {=t1}$ and ${=t1} \div {=d} = {=q1}$ remainder ${=r1}$, so the first decimal digit is ${=q1}$.
$10 \times {=r1} = {=t2}$ and ${=t2} \div {=d} = {=q2}$ remainder ${=r2}$, so the next digit is ${=q2}$.
$10 \times {=r2} = {=t3}$ and ${=t3} \div {=d} = {=q3}$ remainder ${=r3}$, so the next digit is ${=q3}$.

The remainder ${=r1}$ has come back (we also had it after the first digit), so the digits repeat from the second decimal place onwards: the pair ${=q2}{=q3}$ repeats for ever, and $\frac{{=n}}{{=d}} = 0.{=q1}{=q2}{=q3}{=q2}{=q3}{=q2}{=q3}\ldots$
The digit ${=q1}$ comes only once, so it gets no dot. Put a dot over each digit of the repeating pair: $\frac{{=n}}{{=d}} = 0.{=q1}\dot{{=q2}}\dot{{=q3}}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Marks a digit that occurs only once as recurring
proposed_misconceptions.description: Puts the dot or bar over a digit that appears only once before the repeating part (for example writing 3.\overline{136} or 3.\dot{1}\dot{3}\dot{6} for 3.1363636...), because the learner does not locate where the repeat actually begins.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Stops the division before a remainder repeats
proposed_misconceptions.description: Stops the long division after a few digits and writes a truncated or rounded decimal (for example 3.136) instead of recognising the repeating remainder and using recurring notation.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Marks only part of the repeating block
proposed_misconceptions.description: Puts a dot over only the last digit of a two-digit repeating pair (for example 3.13\dot{6} for 3.1363636...), so the notation describes a different number.

notes:
Mirrors book Exercise 1.1 Q11f (4 5/6 = 4.8 with 3 recurring) but with a denominator whose reciprocal is not a known decimal, so long division is required, and with a two-digit repeating pair after one non-repeating digit. Denominators 22, 55, 66 with gcd(n, d) = 1 give exactly one non-repeating digit and a recurring pair, which makes the expansion canonical: the dotted pair starts at the earliest possible place and cannot be shortened. All 70 (d, n) pairs were enumerated and checked against an independent remainder-detection routine; every one gives pre-period [q1] and period [q2, q3], and r3 == r1 always holds, so the six-step solution skeleton is true for every instance (630 instances with the nine whole parts). The non-repeating digit can be 0 (for example 3.0 then a dotted pair); that is correct. Marker convention: the book's own recurring markers store the key in LaTeX (\dot{} / \overline{}), so the marker answer follows that; the stem asks for dot notation, and for a two-digit block dots over each digit equal a bar over the pair, so a bar answer should be accepted as equivalent. Only the advanced gap was authored; basic and standard were not requested.

PIPELINE NORMALISATION (not an author edit): drop-redundant-answer: removed the top-level "answer" ("{=w}.{=q1}\\dot{{=q2}}\\dot{{=q3}}"); an expression family's answer is marker.answer ("{=w}.{=q1}\\dot{{=q2}}\\dot{{=q3}}"), unchanged.
